sentences.text: Nodosaurus is a genus of herbivorous ankylosaurian dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous found only in the Frontier Formation of Wyoming.
This animal grew to roughly 4 to 6 meters long and had bony dermal plates covering its body, possibly with spikes along its sides.
The unique variation in the arrangement of osteoderm rows on the posterior body is known to be exclusive to Nodosaurus.
The genus name means "knotted lizard" in Latin, referring to the bumps on the leg armor.
The species name means "braided" in Latin, referring to the pattern of the armor.
A 2010 estimate by Paul suggests Nodosaurus reached a length of 6 meters and a weight of 3.5 tonnes.
Researchers suggest that without a tail club, Nodosaurus likely defended itself by rolling onto its back to expose only its armored sides and rear, similar to modern hedgehogs.
Fossils of Nodosaurus were first discovered on July 17, 1881, by collector William Harlow Reed in Albany County, Wyoming.
Othniel Charles Marsh scientifically described Nodosaurus and named the species Nodosaurus textilis in 1889.
Nodosaurus is known from two incomplete fossil specimens that lack skulls.
One of the known specimens was found in the Thermopolis Shale of Wyoming.
A third specimen is believed to exist in Mexico, but it has not been confirmed as Nodosaurus.
The holotype, YPM 1815, was found in the Belle Fourche Member of the Frontier Formation.
The holotype consists of a partial skeleton without a skull.

The holotype preserves three back vertebrae, thirteen tail vertebrae, a sacrum, ribs, parts of a scapula, humerus, left elbow and radius, metacarpals, phalanges, both ilia, a left femur, both tibiae, a left perone piece, a left foot, parts of the posterior dorsal armor, a left hip shield, a keeled osteoderm, a vertebral column, and a column-shaped plate.
No other findings have been assigned to the species except for some loose armor plates.
The material was described again by Richard Swann Lull in 1921.
The reconstruction in the publication was the first published reconstruction of a nodosaurid.
In 1978, Walter Preston Coombs renamed taxa as Nodosaurus species, creating Nodosaurus sternbergi and Nodosaurus coleii.
Nodosaurus likely ate soft plants due to its inability to chew tough fibrous ones, or it may have processed tough plants using gastroliths and a large intestinal apparatus.
The class of Nodosaurus is Ornithischia.
The parent group of Nodosaurus is Nodosauridae.
The family of Nodosaurus is Nodosauridae.
The type species of Nodosaurus is Nodosaurus textilis.
Nodosaurus belongs to the subfamily Nodosaurinae within the family Nodosauridae.
Nodosaurus is the homonym of Nodosauridae, one of the two subgroups of Ankylosauria, and is found in this group in most studies.
Vickaryous et al. in 2004 found the findings too scarce for exact classification and listed them as "Ankylosauria incertae sedis".
Marsh originally placed Nodosaurus within Stegosauria in 1889.
In 1890 Marsh named his own family Nodosauridae but thought they were part of the Ceratopsia.
In 1896 Marsh returned Nodosaurus to Stegosauria along with various other armored species.
The holotype dates to the middle Cenomanian, approximately 97 million years ago.
The dating of Nodosaurus has also been given as the Albian.
The time range for Nodosaurus is from the Cenomanian to the Maastrichtian (100.5 to 66 million years ago).
It is debated whether the nodosaurids Stegopelta and Hierosaurus are synonyms of Nodosaurus, a hypothesis proposed in 1978 that has received little support.
